content.comment_body: Hello, I have several basic [product_name] technical questions: For the maximum switching frequency of [product_name] outputs with relay contacts, mechanically, it is limited to 10Hz, and when driving resistive loads, this frequency decreases to 2Hz. 1. Is it possible to reach the 10Hz switching rate if the relay contacts have no current load? 2. Why does the switching frequency drop to 2Hz when current is applied to the contacts? 3. Can it be said that, regardless of the situation—for example, even if all function blocks in the program (say 130 blocks) are used—the relay outputs can still achieve the documented 2Hz rate? Is 2Hz the guaranteed minimum even in a worst-case scenario? 4. Is generating a 1Hz output signal with a 50 percent duty cycle feasible in real time, regardless of program complexity, and even if all available function blocks are used? Thank you. Best regards, [user_name]

Hi, In simple terms, the varying switching times for resistive versus inductive loads occur because inductive loads retain energy, which gets dissipated across the relay contacts when switching off. Therefore, switching too frequently can damage the relays.

analysis.insight_summary: The user is concerned about practical limitations and reliability of relay-based outputs on [product_name], especially regarding their maximum switching frequencies under different load types and program complexities. The main uncertainty is whether the stated frequency limits are guaranteed under all circumstances, such as with a highly complex program or different electrical loads.
analysis.user_expectations: User anticipates reliable output switching at specified rates (up to 10Hz without load, 2Hz with load) regardless of load or program complexity. They want clear assurances and boundaries confirming that the device will consistently perform as specified, even under maximum operational load.
